correctness.rationale: The rank-one tangent projector fixes the off-diagonal control forcing, so the one-step projected Euler state is the unique leading singular component of [[1,u],[u,0]]. Its eigenvalues (1±sqrt(1+4u²))/2 have absolute-value gap exactly one. Exact spectral-projector formulas give the terminal loss. In s=u² the loss derivative has sign T_gamma(sqrt(1+4s))-q, with T_gamma strictly increasing from 1+gamma/2 to infinity for all gamma>=0. This proves the full global-minimizer classification, all boundaries, and the cubic root equation. A Taylor expansion establishes quartic criticality, square-root splitting, objective gain and vanishing Frobenius projection error. The unreduced objective is an explicitly strictly convex quadratic. The executable reproduces 1728 exact rational identities, 2500 parameter tests and 8 asymptotic checks; these supplement rather than replace the proof.

originality.rationale: The compared primary work establishes the dynamical low-rank optimal-control setting and general nonconvexity risk, while earlier projection-method theory specifies rank-retracted Euler steps. Neither statement supplies the one-step target-dependent exact global minimizer count, critical regularization line, global singular gap or near-critical error law. Searches over the exact matrix, equivalent rank-one SVD form, control bifurcation and broad low-rank optimisation aliases did not reveal an equivalent theorem. This is qualified best-knowledge originality, not a claim that nonconvexity itself is new.

value.rationale: A fully characterized smallest nontrivial rank-retracted projected Euler control model changes a strictly convex, uniquely optimized full problem to one with two global controls. The threshold, optimizer scaling and objective gap are exact over the continuous target/regularization domain. Crucially, the singular-value separation is fixed at one and the rank-one residual at the new optima tends to zero at criticality, so this is not a tie or large-retraction-error artifact. The explicit boundary is a useful benchmark for assessing low-rank numerical-control fidelity; no paper-sized downstream theorem is required and no broader solver guarantee is claimed.
